=== page: choices/index.html
title: Choices — The Future of Case Management IT
description: The least conventional decisions in the design, what each is for, and what it costs.

Choices
Several decisions here are not what a team would reach for by default. Each one below says what it buys and what it costs, so you can disagree with it in particular rather than in general.
01 Store dated claims, not facts –
Why it is unusual
Most case systems store the current value of a field and log changes separately.
What it is for
Whether a person owes money back turns on whether the ministry knew something and failed to act. A current value with a change log beside it cannot answer that. The log sits outside the decision path.
What it costs
Every read gets harder. Developers have to think in periods rather than values, and every report has to say which point in time it means.
02 Track two kinds of time, and inherit a third +
Why it is unusual
Finance has modelled two kinds of time for decades. Case management almost never does.
What it is for
A tribunal asks two questions: what was true, and what did the ministry know. Each needs its own axis. The third axis exists because fifteen years of records arrive from a system still in use. Flatten their history into the migration date and a whole class of question stops having an answer.
What it costs
More storage, and a real learning curve. Most inherited records will not know their third date, and the system has to say so rather than guess.
03 Five case models rather than one +
Why it is unusual
The conventional move is a single configurable case model shared across programs.
What it is for
A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal share almost nothing. A shared model turns every change into a negotiation. The last programme cut scope rather than reopen one.
What it costs
The plumbing gets written five times. That is a real cost, and the design accepts it on purpose.
04 Decisions read no live data +
Why it is unusual
Teams usually call the rules engine as a service, and it fetches what it needs while it runs.
What it is for
A decision that reads anything not stored with it cannot be re-run. Re-running is what lets you show a tribunal what happened, rather than piece it together from memory.
What it costs
Someone has to gather the facts before the decision runs, and gathering them consistently is a problem of its own.
05 The interface outlives its implementation +
Why it is unusual
Teams normally treat the translation layer over a legacy system as the lasting asset.
What it is for
Replacing a system in pieces only works if nobody calling it can tell which piece answered. The published interface is permanent. The translation layer behind it is temporary, and its team answers for winding itself up.
What it costs
The published interface has to refuse old vocabulary, even on the days when exposing it would be faster.
06 Store the letter, not just the decision +
Why it is unusual
Most systems treat letters as output rather than as part of the record.
What it is for
A tribunal asks what the person was told as often as it asks what the system worked out. A decision that re-runs perfectly, next to a letter nobody can rebuild, still misses the question.
What it costs
Template versions and content hashes have to survive as long as the decisions that point at them.
07 Retention lives on the type, not the storage location +
Why it is unusual
Most systems work out how long to keep something from where it sits.
What it is for
Guessing from location fails the first time a fact appears in two places, which is day one. Attach the classification and the retention rule to the kind of evidence instead. Then destroying records becomes a job you can actually do.
What it costs
Every evidence type needs a records ruling before anyone can use it, which puts the records office on the critical path.
How the design was arrived at
This architecture rests on every document we could recover about ICM and the work it supports. Each claim traces back to a primary source, or the documents confirm it between themselves, or the arithmetic gives it. Claims we could not check say so on the page.
The design began with the assumptions that ICM rested on, and much of the approach to MIS with it. We tested eleven. None came through intact. Two of them:
System residency is a legal requirement
No federal or provincial statute says government systems have to sit in Canada. No published policy says it either.
Worries about data sovereignty and trade still point to keeping the systems in Canada, and the architecture does that. No formal guidance stands behind the choice.
Replacing the existing system has a deadline
The vendor has committed to support the current platform to at least December 2037, on a rolling ten-year basis.
Nothing outside the programme forces the replacement to finish by a set date. So it can do discovery, research and analysis properly before it commits to building at scale. An unforced timetable takes a great deal of risk out of the work.
Two of the eleven assumptions that did not survive testing.
What the evidence base is
Two bodies of source material sit behind this. The first is 57 technical design documents for the current release. They cover the application, its integrations, its data conversion and its reporting. The second is 326 service-delivery procedures, describing how the work gets done.
Reading both matters, because they disagree about what the system is. The technical documents describe 61 applications. The procedures turn up 28 more tools that a worker touches and no technical document mentions. Among them: a standalone calculator, a reporting tool, credit and asset-check portals, a worker-safety device, a vital statistics service.
What remains unresolved
The architecture carries 40 open items to verify, and 30 more to settle before the design freezes. Three are worth naming here, because they change the shape of the work rather than its detail:
Whether the rules can move off the mainframe on their own, given that both of them calculate.
Whether we can settle what the third time axis holds before the first production record lands. Nobody can add it afterwards.
What service levels the analytical platform can promise. That waits on a storage benchmark nobody has run yet.
DRAFT
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.
Figures on this site are drawn from the architecture document and from 326 service-delivery procedures. Nothing here is a government commitment.

Current State
This design does not set out to contradict the current system. It comes from one question. Why does a large, expensive piece of software, laboured over by hundreds of capable and well-meaning people, still fail the organizations it serves? The answer lies in what the system leaves out: what it ignores, and what it pushes outside itself.
What the SDPR procedures are
Every recurring task a caseworker does has a written procedure: what starts it, which screens to open, which form to send, what to type in which field. Together they run to 8.2 million characters. They describe the service as staff really deliver it.
Each one carries a header naming its purpose, the policy it carries out, the law behind it, and how the system classifies the work. That turns the whole set into a map of the services.
326procedures
15capability areas
128kinds of work request
84statutory provisions cited
146distinct forms
13ways to reach the ministry
Work crosses system boundaries constantly
63% of documented procedures need two or more systems to finish one task.
Number of procedures by count of separate systems required, across 326 procedures.
Systems
Procedures
Proportion
0
39
1
80
2
114
3
51
4+
42
Highlighted rows are the 207 procedures that cross a system boundary. Four procedures require seven.
Counted by naming every system referenced in each procedure. The most common pairing is the Siebel case system with the client portal, then the case system with Service Canada, then the case system with the mainframe.
One journey, three systems, two re-keys
Recovering an overpayment is the clearest example. A worker who has decided someone was paid too much has to:
Open a separate web application to calculate the amount. It does not connect to either system of record.
Print the result, scan it, and attach it back to the case.
Move the case file to their own office in the mainframe so they have permission to act on it.
Type the amount into the mainframe by hand.
Move the case file back to where it came from.
Clients whose earnings are annualised need one step more: a spreadsheet. The worker reads figures off one screen, types them into the sheet, and types the result back.
None of this is anyone's poor practice. The procedure says to do it this way, because with the systems that exist this is the right way.
Where the rules actually live
A modernisation has to know what it is replacing. The rules that decide entitlement sit in four separate places, and only one of them is a rules engine.
Business rules by location
Where
What it holds
A rules engine
29 separate rulebases covering eligibility, validation, debt and payment calculation
The mainframe
Benefit calculation, rate recalculation, time limits, sanction end dates
Formulas inside the case system
Retention periods, access levels, privacy calculations
A database table
The rates the public-facing eligibility estimator uses
Found by reading the technical design documents for the current release alongside the procedures. Nothing on record gives the 29 rulebases source control, a promotion pipeline or a version register.
Routing runs on a spreadsheet
An Excel workbook decides which queue a request joins, how urgent it is, how long it has, and where a scanned document goes. Fifty-six procedures point at it. One of its sheets maps 445 form numbers to their handling. So the priorities and service-level targets for the whole service sit outside the platform, kept up by hand.
Accommodation and the signature problem
There is a path for applicants who need an interpreter, find reading difficult, or have little access to a computer. A worker reads the questions aloud and enters the answers for them.
That path skips portal registration, so the applicant never gets a personal identification number. The electronic signature depends on that number. So the people the accommodation exists for are the people who then cannot sign electronically.
How these figures were produced
The counts come from reading the Resource Finder and the other document stores in full, then pattern-matching and mapping the text. Named systems, capability areas and the policy behind each procedure come from the documents and the policy manual.
Nobody has measured the volumes yet. You can count caseload throughput, worker streams, transaction rates and queue depth directly. The figures here come from the technical design documents instead.
The rest of the site sets out how the design answers these conditions. Start with evidence. The overpayment journey above follows directly from a record that cannot say what the ministry knew, or when.

=== page: determinations/index.html
title: Determinations — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why an entitlement decision is treated as a function that can be re-run years later.

Determinations
Someone can challenge a decision about their entitlement years after the ministry made it. So the design treats every decision as something you re-run, not something you remember.
The problem with asking a system what it decided
Ask a typical case management system why a person got a particular amount in March 2022 and it will work the sum again. It uses today's rules, today's data and today's software, then reports the answer with confidence. The answer may well be right. Nobody can tell, and nobody can show a tribunal the difference.
Three things have shifted underneath since March 2022. Policy changed. The person's recorded circumstances changed, perhaps several times. And someone upgraded the software. A rules engine upgrade can change how the same rule reads, and nobody notices until a client appeals.
Treating a decision as a function
The design makes entitlement a calculation with no hidden inputs. It reads the rules, the facts and the date it is deciding for. While it runs it does not read the clock, query a database, or call another service. It gets everything it needs up front.
That rule sounds academic. It is what makes the next part work: if nothing hidden went in, then storing what went in is enough to reproduce what came out.
The function signature
Determine(rulesArtefactVersion, evidenceSnapshot, referenceDate) → DeterminationResult
Pure: no input or output, no clock reads, no database access, no service calls. No rules engine gives you this on its own. The shell around the engine enforces it. The engine runs in-process against a snapshot passed by value, and that is what puts byte-identical replay within reach rather than in the brochure.
Five things stored with every decision
Storing the answer is not enough. Storing the answer and the rules is still not enough. The system binds five artefacts into the record at the moment it makes the decision.
1 The rules Content digest, tagged and immutable once released Stored
2 The engine Version number and the archived binary Stored
3 The facts it saw Copied in full into the record, never referenced Stored
4 The reasoning Which rules fired and which branches were taken, in a ministry-owned format Stored
5 The letter Content-hashed template, resolved at decision time Stored
The decision can be replayed.
Four years on, the same inputs produce the same answer, the reasoning can be read aloud, and the letter the client received can be reproduced.
Switch any artefact off to see which question stops being answerable. Each one covers a failure the other four do not.
Teams leave out the fifth one most often. A decision that reproduces perfectly, next to a letter nobody can rebuild, still misses the question the tribunal asked. That question is often about what the person was told, not about what the system worked out.
How long replay has to work
Archiving the software tells you what it was. It does not promise that anything in twenty years can still run it. The operating system, the processor and the container runtime all die younger than a child protection record, which the ministry keeps for ninety years.
Rather than leave that hanging, the design commits to a horizon in three stages and writes it down in advance.
Years 0–7
We archive the software itself and test it every quarter to confirm it still runs. Seven years covers the appeal, reconsideration and audit paths that really do re-run a decision.
Years 7–20
The rules live on as a written specification, with a test suite that any rebuild has to pass. The suite stays independent of the engine from day one, so this handover costs nothing when it comes.
Beyond 20 years
The stored reasoning, the letter and the facts are the record. Re-running stops being on offer. This is what a paper file has always been.
The three stages run in order, which is why they are numbered. The last one holds up because the ministry declared it in advance, rather than discovering it during a hearing.
Two decisions made moments apart can disagree
Storing the inputs makes replay reliable. It says nothing about whether the inputs were gathered consistently. That is where the remaining gap sits.
Gathering the facts means reading across several stores that update on their own schedules. Two decisions issued seconds apart, with one store briefly behind, can each see a different world quite legitimately. Both replay perfectly. Both are reproducible. They disagree, and nothing described so far catches it. So the design pins each snapshot to a point in the sequence of recorded events. A later reader can then tell which view of the world a decision was made against.
Decisions that affect people carry their own classification
Every rule carries a label saying what kind of decision it produces. Some produce an administrative decision, which needs reasons. Some produce a decision a person has to make before it takes effect. The rest are working sums that affect nobody on their own.
That label travels with the decision into the letter. A decision that goes against someone sends out its reasons, its appeal period and the route to challenge it, because the label says it must. Not because somebody remembered.
DRAFT
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.

=== page: domains/index.html
title: Domains — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why the design uses sixteen separate models rather than one, and the rules that keep them separate.

Domains
Perhaps the biggest choice in this design is where to draw the lines between parts of the system. Twelve domain models, one of which is really five sub-domains, which makes sixteen.
The problem of a single model
Programmes like this usually start by building one model of a case that every program can share. That is how MIS began, and how ICM began. It looks like the responsible choice: less duplication, one place to change things, one way of working across the ministry.
What happens next is well documented. A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal have almost nothing in common beyond involving a person. Make them share a lifecycle and every change to one has to be negotiated with everyone else. Multiply that over dozens of programs and nobody can change the model at all. So teams bolt on sub-entities, extend them, and add more ways to integrate. The system turns into a plate of spaghetti. You cannot change anything in one place, and any failure reaches everywhere. This is not hypothetical. ICM merged its final two phases and cut child protection scope for exactly this reason.
This design takes the difference seriously. Five program families get five case models. The plumbing is written more than once, and that is cheaper than the alternative.
What the parts are
Shared spine
Participant Identity
Evidence & Verification
Eligibility & Entitlement
One per program family
Employment assistance
Child protection
Child care subsidy
Employment services
Persons with disabilities
Money
Payments & Issuance
Financial Components
Overpayment & Recovery
Delivery
Appeals & Reconsideration
Work Management
Documents & Capture
Notices & Correspondence
Provider & Outcome
Evidence & Verification
Every dated claim about the world, and how it was checked.
Owns
The evidence succession set, verification policy, the four operations, three time axes.
Does not own
It does not decide anything. It records what was claimed and what was verified.
Boundary test
Its events are the trigger fabric for everything else.
Select any part to see what it owns, what it deliberately does not own, and the test that tells you when the boundary has been breached. The five case models share protocols, not a case model.
Four rules keep the lines in place
A boundary that lives only in a diagram will not survive delivery pressure. These four are written so a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies.
Each part can be released on its own
It has its own storage and its own message topics. If two parts always ship together, they are one part wearing two names.
No part reads another part's database
No shared tables. No joins across schemas. Not for a report, and not in a test environment. This rule erodes first, and takes the longest to notice.
There are exactly two ways to talk
A published interface for reads, and published events for notices. There is no third way, and adding one is not a shortcut.
Copies are owned by whoever holds them
A part that needs another's data keeps its own copy, built from that part's events and shaped the way it needs. When the source corrects something, the copy has to follow.
The thin identity model
Participant Identity stays deliberately small. It holds identifiers, enough detail to tell two people apart, and whether anyone has proven the identity. No addresses, no income, no relationships.
This part is the most likely to drift, because every new requirement brings a reason to add one more field to the person record. Once that starts, the shared model is back, in the one place the design most needs to stay thin.
Merge and split go in on day one rather than later. The audit of the previous system found duplicate records at scale, and called its search ineffective and exact-match only. Adding merge afterwards to a system that assumed one person equals one row is close to impossible. By then every payment instruction and every stored decision has keyed itself to an identifier the design promised would hold still.
Published events and the boundary test
Participant Identity publishes PersonRegistered, IdentityMerged, IdentitySplit, IdentifierAdded and IdentifierInvalidated. Every other context keeps its own projection (Payee, Applicant, Caregiver, Reporter, Appellant, Debtor), keyed by participant identifier.
Evidence & Verification publishes EvidenceRecorded, EvidenceActivated, EvidenceSuperseded, EvidenceVerified, EvidenceInvalidated and EvidenceCorrectionRecorded.
Parts that are not domain models
Some pieces are shared infrastructure rather than parts of the business. Platform teams own them and everyone uses them. The difference matters. A platform part that starts holding program state has quietly become a seventeenth domain model, and nobody chartered it.
Two of them are worth naming, because their charters point in opposite directions on purpose. The published interface is permanent: it is the contract built to outlive whatever implements it. The translation layer over the existing Siebel system is temporary, and the team that builds it answers for winding itself up.
A team accountable for a thing will grow and protect it. A team measured on its own dissolution will not.
DRAFT
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.

=== page: evidence/index.html
title: Evidence — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why the system records dated claims rather than facts, and why it tracks two kinds of time.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview

Glossary
Evidence
ICM tracks facts. It overwrites fields and buries history. In the new system the unit of information is a dated claim, tied to its evidence and to whoever made it. Later work can disprove that claim, confirm it, overturn it or replace it, and nothing is lost on the way.
Why not store facts?
A system that stores only the current state, "Income: $900", leaves the important questions open. How do we know? What evidence is there? When did we know? Is this the corrected number, or the number we recorded at the time?
Front-line staff adapt, so the information is not lost. It is just not modelled. It goes into notes, forms and attachments, and only a thin slice of it is ever held as data.
This is not an auditing nicety. It closes the gap between how the system holds data and how front-line staff work. Substantiating evidence against claims is the most common task a worker performs, and the system does not model it at all, so it is done by hand. Social workers spend hours mapping their notes onto a structure that serves the software rather than their clients.
So the unit of storage is an assertion:
what household composition: couple
about whomparticipant 4471-A
true forfrom 1 January, open-ended
learned on12 September
fromeligibility review finding
verifiedtenancy agreement, 14 September
One evidence assertion, from a case where the dates are in dispute. The ministry now says the household was a couple from January. It reached that view in September. In between it paid eight months at the single rate. Which of those two dates you read decides what happens next.
The four things that can happen to an assertion
Once the system records something, nobody edits it in place. Four operations change what the system believes. They differ in one respect: what each does to the period the claim covers.
[aria-label] Evidence operations
Record
Supersede
Correct
Invalidate
The world changed.
valid time
a new period
transaction time
now
The earlier assertion stays true for its own period. The new one takes over from a later date.
For example A partner moves in on 1 May, and the client reports it.
If this produced an overpayment, the classification rule reads the operation as the world having changed.
Select an operation. Supersede and Correct both replace an earlier claim, but only Correct says the earlier claim was wrong about its own period. That is what separates a recoverable debt from the ministry's own error.
That distinction is why the model exists. It is a policy rule written into the shape of the data. It applies consistently because the record itself names the operation that caused the recalculation. Nobody has to guess at it afterwards.
The operation feeds the classification without settling it. Who caused the error matters too. A client who hid a relationship is not in the same position as a worker who mis-keyed a figure. The model promises something narrower and more useful: the question has an answer at all, and the answer comes from the record rather than from whoever opens the file today.
Where a conventional record gives up
Take the assertion above to a tribunal. The client accepts a relationship exists but disputes that it began in January. Three separate things are now in question, and they are easy to confuse:
What the ministry believed about the household in each of those eight months.
When the ministry changed its mind, and on what evidence.
What start date the ministry now asserts.
A conventional design holds one relationship start date, plus an audit entry saying a worker changed it on 12 September. That answers the third question, gestures at the second, and cannot touch the first. It leaves the eight monthly payments looking like errors. Each one was the right answer to what the ministry knew at the time.
The operations, formally
Operation
Valid time
Transaction time
Meaning
RecordEvidence
asserted period
now
We learned a new fact
SupersedeEvidence
new period
now
The world changed
CorrectEvidence
same period
now
We were wrong about the world
InvalidateEvidence
closed
now
The assertion should never have existed
The aggregate is the evidence succession set: the stream of versions of one logical fact about one subject. Commands append events; current state is a projection. Verification status transitions are themselves events.
The third date, and the history problem
Two time axes are standard. This design carries a third, because the new system inherits fifteen years of records from systems that are still running.
Old records all arrive on the same day. Make that migration date the "when we learned it" date and every historical fact looks as though it arrived at the same moment. Supersede and Correct then look identical across the whole pre-cutover record. The overpayment rule stops working on exactly the records where most overpayments sit.
The third axis holds the date the old system asserted the fact, where the old record still shows it. Often it cannot be read at all, so the date carries a confidence marker. Where the answer is unknown, the system says so rather than guessing.
valid time
The period in the world for which the fact holds.
Set by whoever asserts it, from the source.
transaction time
When this system learned it.
Set at recording. Never changes.
legacy assertion time
When the previous system asserted it, if that can be decoded.
Set at migration. Often unknown, and marked as such.
Three dates on every assertion. The third can be empty, and the design treats an unknown value as unknown rather than swapping in the migration date.
Nobody can add this later. Events are immutable: you can introduce a field with a default, but you cannot fill it in afterwards. Either the migration decoded the source or it did not. So the decision has to come before the first production record.
Confidence values and replay behaviour
legacy_asserted_at travels with legacy_assertion_confidence, which takes DECODED (read straight from the legacy record or audit trail), INFERRED (worked out from a related artefact by a written rule) or UNKNOWN.
On UNKNOWN, any consumer working out a knowledge-state answer must return INDETERMINATE. That covers the overpayment rule, a tribunal reconstruction view and a disclosure history. Projections that answer only valid-time questions ignore the field.
Backdated recalculation runs off valid time, which any competent migration preserves, so recalculation survives. Something narrower breaks without the third axis: what the ministry knew and when. That is the question separating a recoverable debt from the ministry's own error.
DRAFT
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.

Glossary
The parameters and requirements use some words that have a particular meaning in this work. This page explains each one in plain terms. Where architects have their own name for an idea, it is given in brackets, so you can recognise it in other documents.
[aria-label] Jump to a letter
A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H
I
J
K
L
M
N
O
P
R
S
T
V
W
Accessibility standard
The rules a screen or form must follow so that people with disabilities can use it.
The Province sets a standard for how accessible its online services must be. It is based on the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), an international set of rules. They cover things like text a screen reader can read aloud, colours with enough contrast, and forms you can fill in with a keyboard alone.
N15 asks for this from the first release, not as a fix added later.
Used in:
[aria-label] N15: Everyone can use the service, whatever their ability or way in
N15 In requirements: BR-009 · NFR-U-002
Active-active
Running a service at two or more sites at once, so either can carry the load if the other fails.
In requirements: NFR-A-004
Adjudicability
Four facts recorded for each entitlement: whether it is granted under a statute, whether its decisions can be reconsidered, whether they can be appealed, and to whom.
In requirements: FR-006 · FR-030 · FR-033 · FR-056 · FR-063 · FR-092
Adjudicating authority
A body allowed to decide or review a class of decisions. It can be inside the ministry or outside it, such as Pacific Blue Cross or CLBC.
In requirements: FR-056
Adverse decision
A decision that denies, reduces or ends assistance, or creates a debt.
Aggregate
A cluster of data the system treats as one unit for changes, with its own rules that must always hold.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-011
API, REST, GraphQL
An API is how systems ask each other for data or actions; REST and GraphQL are two common styles.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-002 · NFR-I-003 · INT-003
Appeal
Asking an independent body outside the ministry to look at a decision again.
If a client still disagrees after a reconsideration, they can often appeal. An appeal goes to a body outside the ministry, usually a tribunal. Not every decision can be appealed, and not every appeal goes to the same body. That is why N20 records this for each entitlement.
Used in:
[aria-label] N17: Different people decide, review and pay
N17 ·
[aria-label] N20: Each benefit records whether and how a decision can be challenged
N20
Appeal record
Everything the ministry had in front of it when it made a decision, gathered for the client.
When a client challenges a decision, policy says the ministry must give them the appeal record. It holds all the submissions, information and records the ministry had when it made the decision. Before the client gets it, some protected details may have to be removed. That step is called severing.
N08 asks that the system can put this record together on demand, rather than staff searching for the pieces by hand.
Used in:
[aria-label] N08: The decision record is complete on its own
N08
Asserted negative
A question asked and answered "no". It counts as evidence, unlike a blank that was never asked.
In requirements: FR-011 · DR-002
Assisted digital
A worker or representative completing an online transaction for someone, with the helper's identity recorded.
Assistive technology
Tools people with disabilities use to work a computer or phone, such as screen readers.
Examples are screen readers that read the page aloud, software that magnifies the screen, voice control, and switches used instead of a mouse. Automated scans find only about 30% of accessibility problems. The rest show up only when a person tries the service with these tools, which is why N15 asks for real testing.
Used in:
[aria-label] N15: Everyone can use the service, whatever their ability or way in
N15 In requirements: BR-009 · NFR-U-002
Automated check
A test that software runs by itself to catch a rule being broken.
Technical teams use several kinds. A lint rule reads the code and flags patterns that break a rule, such as one part reaching into another part’s tables. A fitness function is a test of the whole design, run again and again, that fails if the design drifts away from a goal. A compatibility check compares a new version of an interface with the old one and fails if the change would break anyone who uses it.
N18 says that wherever a rule can be checked this way, it must be. A person then only has to check what a machine cannot.
Used in:
[aria-label] N18: Every rule comes with a way to catch it being broken
N18 In requirements: NFR-A-003 · NFR-M-004
Availability target
How much of the time a service must be up and working.
It is usually given as a percentage over a month or a year. A service that must be available 99.9% of the time can be down for about 45 minutes a month. N16 asks that each service’s target be set by how much harm an outage does to a client, not picked the same for everything.
Used in:
[aria-label] N16: Each service has recovery targets, proven in practice runs
N16 In requirements: NFR-A-007 · INT-005
Back end for front end
A small server behind each user interface that holds the sign-in tokens, so they never sit in the browser.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-001 · INT-005
BCEA Policy and Procedure Manual
The ministry's published policy manual for employment and disability assistance. Under the source hierarchy it overrides procedures and job aids, and legislation overrides it.
In requirements: BR-007 · BR-013 · BR-014
BCeID, BC Services Card, IDIR
Provincial sign-in credentials: BCeID for individuals and businesses, the BC Services Card for citizens with verified identity, and IDIR for government staff.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-001 · INT-005
Benefit component
One part of an assistance payment, such as support, shelter or a supplement. Each component can take effect on a different date.
In requirements: FR-005
Break-glass access
Emergency access to a restricted record outside normal rules, always logged and reviewed afterwards.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-004
Business rule
A rule about how the ministry’s work is done, such as who qualifies for a benefit.
Business rules come from law, policy and practice. “A client must report income by the fifth of the month” is one. N04 asks that each rule lives in one place, with the data it controls, so there is never a question about which copy of the rule is the real one.
Used in:
[aria-label] N04: Rules live with the data they control
N04
Byte-identical
Exactly the same, down to every character, with nothing that differs.
Calendar basis
Which calendar a time limit counts in, such as business days, calendar months or the school year.
In requirements: FR-024 · FR-039 · FR-061
Capture, states S0–S3
Moving a part of the service to the new system for a cohort, through four states: old system in charge (S0), shadow (S1), captured with write-back (S2), new system in charge (S3).
In requirements: DR-014
CFCSA
The Child, Family and Community Service Act, BC's child protection law. Section 96 lets child protection workers request information.
In requirements: INT-013
Channel
A way a person reaches the ministry: online, by phone, in person or by mail.
N15 asks that a person can finish the same task through every supported channel and get the same result. It also asks that every service has a supported way in that is not online.
Used in:
[aria-label] N15: Everyone can use the service, whatever their ability or way in
N15
Child in the Home of a Relative (CIHR)
A closed program supporting children living with relatives. It runs on rules frozen in 2010 alongside the current rules.
In requirements: FR-010 · FR-023 · INT-013
CI (continuous integration)
The automated pipeline that builds and tests every change before it can be released.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-002 · NFR-U-002 · NFR-M-004 · NFR-I-002
Circuit breaker, bulkhead, timeout
Protections that stop one failing service from taking others down with it.
In requirements: NFR-P-001 · NFR-A-003
Client index
A single index for finding people and spotting duplicate records, with uncertain matches sent to a person to decide.
In requirements: FR-028 · INT-016 · DR-019
Cohort review
Holding a large group of new debts that share one cause for review before any notices go out.
Common tools
Tools almost every organisation needs, like sign-in and document storage, that can be bought rather than built.
N11 lists them: workflow (moving work between people), notifications, identity and sign-in, storing passwords and encryption keys safely, policy checks (software that decides whether an action is allowed), scheduling, document storage, search, and print and mail.
Good products for all of these already exist. Building one in-house is allowed only for a need no product meets, and someone outside the team has to agree.
Used in:
[aria-label] N11: Buy common tools, and have someone else check any choice to build
N11
Component library (tiered)
Shared, reusable interface building blocks, split into tiers so accessibility logic sits in the shared lower tiers.
In requirements: NFR-U-005
Considered but not retainable
Evidence that policy lets staff look at but not keep, such as tax information that must not be printed.
In requirements: DR-002
Control totals
Counts and sums struck before a run is approved and checked unchanged afterwards.
In requirements: BR-007 · FR-043 · NFR-C-003 · NFR-M-003 · DR-004
Copy
A fact one part of the system holds that it took from another part.
Parts of the system often keep their own copy of a fact so they can work quickly without asking the source every time. That is normal. The risk is that the source corrects the fact and the copy stays wrong. N06 asks that every copy records where it came from, so a correction can always find it.
Used in:
[aria-label] N06: Every copy can be traced, and every correction reaches it
N06 ·
[aria-label] N21: Limits on how information may be used travel with it
N21 In requirements: NFR-C-004
Corporate Accounting System (CAS)
The Province's financial system of record. All payments are posted and reconciled against it.
In requirements: BR-004 · FR-042 · NFR-A-005 · NFR-S-003 · NFR-C-008 · INT-001
Correction
Fixing a fact that was recorded wrongly, as opposed to a fact that changed.
These two are easy to confuse, and they mean different things. A correction says the record was wrong all along: the income was never $900, it was $1,100. An update, sometimes called a supersession, says the world changed: the income was $900 until March and $1,100 after.
The difference matters for money. A correction can mean a client was underpaid or overpaid in the past. An update does not. The old system cannot tell the two apart, which is why N14 says that difference is lost if a group moves back.

N06 ·
[aria-label] N14: Every move can be undone, and what is lost is written down
N14 In requirements: FR-012 · FR-051 · DR-001 · DR-015
Correlation identifier
An ID carried through every step of a request so its whole path can be traced afterwards.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-010 · NFR-C-001 · NFR-M-001
CPP, OAS, GIS, EI, SIN
Federal programs and identifiers: Canada Pension Plan, Old Age Security, Guaranteed Income Supplement, Employment Insurance, and the Social Insurance Number.
In requirements: FR-027 · NFR-P-001 · INT-007
Custodian
The organisation responsible for a record and entitled to decide how it is used.
Most records the ministry holds are the provincial government’s. Some are not. A record may belong to an Indigenous Nation or another organisation and be held by the ministry under an agreement. N13 asks that the system stores who the custodian is and acts on it, rather than relying on staff to know.
Used in:
[aria-label] N13: The system knows whose record it is
N13 In requirements: BR-008 · FR-084 · NFR-SEC-005 · NFR-C-007 · DR-005
Data load (migration)
Moving existing records from the old system into the new one.
Migration scripts copy large amounts of data in bulk. If a rule is enforced only by the screens staff use, a bulk load can skip right past it. N04 asks that the data enforce its own rules, so every route in is checked.
Used in:
[aria-label] N04: Rules live with the data they control
N04
Data model
A part’s own description of the things it works with, such as a person or a payment.
Different parts of the ministry’s work need to know different things about the same person. Payments needs a bank account. Intake needs contact details. A single shared model tries to hold all of it, and every change then needs everyone to agree.
N03 asks each part to keep its own model instead. The Domains page shows the sixteen parts and what each one owns.
See it at work: Domains Used in:
[aria-label] N03: Each part keeps its own picture of the data
N03
Data-sharing agreement
A formal agreement setting out what information one organisation may share with another, and why.
Today these agreements are usually signed documents. Staff read them and then set up access by hand. N13 asks that each agreement is also written in a form the system can read, and that the system grants access from the agreement itself. That way every access can be traced to an agreement and checked.
Used in:
[aria-label] N13: The system knows whose record it is
N13 In requirements: BR-006 · BR-008 · FR-085
Database layout (schema)
The structure of a database: its tables, its columns, and what each one holds.
Technical teams call this a schema. When one part sends another a copy of its database rows, or relies on its layout, the two become tied together. Neither can change its layout without breaking the other. N02, N03 and N10 all guard against this.
Used in:
[aria-label] N02: Parts of the system share facts and decisions, not raw data
N02 ·
[aria-label] N03: Each part keeps its own picture of the data
N03 ·
[aria-label] N10: The interface outlasts the system behind it
N10 In requirements: NFR-I-003
Date conflict (rule status)
A rule that the policy manual gives two different effective dates. It cannot be released until the ministry rules on which date is right.
De-identified, synthetic, differentially private data
Data changed so people cannot be identified: identifiers removed, made up to look realistic, or blurred with statistical noise.
In requirements: FR-045 · NFR-P-002 · NFR-SEC-012 · NFR-C-004 · DR-017
Decision (determination)
The system working out what a client is entitled to under the rules.
Architects call this a determination. The system takes the facts about a client and the rules for a benefit, and works out the result: eligible or not, and how much. N07, N08 and N09 are all about making that calculation something you can repeat and explain.
See it at work: Determinations Used in:
[aria-label] N07: The calculation uses only what it is given
N07 In requirements: FR-001 · FR-011 · FR-025 · FR-042 · FR-051 · FR-057 · FR-062 · FR-073and 12 more
Decision class (A, B, C)
How a rule output is treated: A is an administrative decision needing reasons, B needs a human decision-maker before it is issued, C is an intermediate calculation never shown as a decision.
In requirements: FR-003
Decision record
The stored account of a decision: what was decided, on what facts, under which rules.
Every decision the system makes is saved with everything needed to explain it later. That includes the version of the rules, the facts it used, what the client asked for, which requirements were and were not met, and when the client was told.
N08 asks that the record holds full copies of all of this, not links to other systems. That way it still makes sense years later, after those systems have changed or gone.

N17 In requirements: BR-005 · FR-001 · FR-051 · FR-058 · FR-062 · FR-095 · NFR-A-006 · NFR-SEC-009and 1 more
Decision trace
The step-by-step record of which rules fired and with what values, in a format the ministry owns.
In requirements: BR-008 · FR-002
Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act
The B.C. law that commits the Province to bring its laws in line with the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
Passed in 2019, often shortened to DRIPA or the Declaration Act. The UN Declaration recognises Indigenous peoples’ right to govern their own affairs, and that includes information about their own people. A ministry system that treats every record as the Province’s cannot honour that. This is the reason for N13.
Used in:
[aria-label] N13: The system knows whose record it is
N13 In requirements: BR-008
Deemed receipt
The date a notice is treated as received, set by rule. The client's time to challenge counts from it.
In requirements: FR-064 · INT-003
Degraded mode
A planned, reduced way of working when a dependency fails.
In requirements: NFR-A-003
Delegated agency
An organisation, including Indigenous agencies, authorised to deliver child and family services on the ministry's behalf.
In requirements: INT-013
Design freeze
The point after which the design is fixed and building starts. Several decisions must be made before it.
In requirements: BR-013 · NFR-P-001 · NFR-S-001
Destroying records (disposition)
What happens to a record at the end of its life: destroyed, archived or handed over.
Records cannot be kept forever. The law sets how long each kind must be kept and what happens after. Architects call this disposition. A record may be destroyed, moved to the archives, or handed to another government that is its rightful custodian.
N12 asks that the way each kind of record ends is decided before the system stores anything, because the method shapes how the records are stored.
Used in:
[aria-label] N12: How records are destroyed is decided before anything is stored
N12 ·
[aria-label] N13: The system knows whose record it is
N13 In requirements: FR-072 · FR-096 · NFR-C-003
Destroying the key (crypto-shredding)
Locking one person’s records with their own key, then destroying the key to make the records unreadable.
Each person’s records are scrambled (encrypted) with a key that belongs to them alone. When the records must be destroyed, the system destroys the key. The scrambled data can stay in place, but nobody can read it ever again. This lets a permanent history meet a legal duty to destroy.
It is one of three ways N12 lists. It needs careful planning about who holds the keys and how destruction is proven.
Used in:
[aria-label] N12: How records are destroyed is decided before anything is stored
N12 In requirements: NFR-S-002 · NFR-SEC-005 · DR-004
Discretionary determination
A decision a person makes using judgement, recorded with their identity, authority and reasons.
In requirements: FR-047
Driver (DRV-)
The reason a requirement exists: a law, the policy manual, the nature of the work, or an aim of the architecture.
Duty to accommodate
The Human Rights Code duty to adjust service for a person's needs, such as disability or language, unless there is a clear and justifiable reason it cannot be met.
In requirements: BR-009 · FR-087
EA Act and EAPWD Act
The Employment and Assistance Act and the Employment and Assistance for Persons with Disabilities Act, with their regulations. They set who qualifies for assistance and how much.
In requirements: FR-030
Effective date
The date a rule, rate or decision takes effect. It is often different from the date it was published or made.
Emergency issuance
A designed way to pay people when the normal decision process is down, using the same controls and settled later.
In requirements: FR-047 · NFR-C-008
Entitlement
A specific benefit or payment a client may qualify for.
A programme such as income assistance contains many separate entitlements: a monthly support amount, a shelter amount, and dozens of supplements for things like transportation, dental care or a special diet. Each can have its own rules, its own law behind it, and its own route to challenge a decision. Eligibility is whether a client qualifies for an entitlement, and from what date.
Used in:
[aria-label] N17: Different people decide, review and pay

N20
Entitlement clock, service-standard clock
A breach of an entitlement clock changes what the client is owed; a breach of a service-standard clock does not.
In requirements: FR-061
Error attribution
Who caused a recorded mistake: the client, the ministry, a third party, or unknown. It must be recorded with every correction.
Event
A single thing the system records as having happened, such as a fact recorded or a decision issued.
The new system keeps its history as a long list of events, each added to the end and never changed. “The first event” means the first real record the new system stores. Several parameters must be in place before that moment, because once events exist in one shape they cannot be reshaped.

N19 In requirements: NFR-P-001 · NFR-A-006 · NFR-SEC-009 · NFR-M-001 · NFR-I-004 · INT-023
Evidence programme
The first 90 days of the programme, used to test assumptions and settle early decisions. "Day 45" and "Day 90" count from its start.
Evidence tier (E1–E4)
Levels of proof kept about cross-organisation exchanges, from basic attributable logs (E1) to signed messages (E4).
In requirements: NFR-SEC-010 · INT-022
Excision test
Removing the product behind an interface and counting how many interface changes that forces. The target is zero.
In requirements: NFR-I-001
Fact (evidence)
A piece of information about a client that someone has claimed is true, such as their income.
In the new system a fact is never just a value like “$1,100”. It is a claim: who said it, what period it covers, and when the system learned it. The site also calls facts evidence, because they are what a decision rests on.
The Evidence page shows how this works, with a worked example.

N08 In requirements: FR-014 · FR-073 · NFR-A-002
FMEP
The Family Maintenance Enforcement Program, which collects court-ordered support. The ministry must disclose some debtor information to it on request.
In requirements: INT-024
FOIPPA
The Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, B.C.’s main privacy and access law.
It gives people the right to see records the government holds, including records about themselves. It also protects other people’s personal information. When the ministry releases a record, FOIPPA decides which details must be removed first.
Used in:
[aria-label] N08: The decision record is complete on its own
N08 In requirements: FR-058 · FR-076 · NFR-C-001
Group of clients
A set of clients moved from the old system to the new one together.
The new system will not replace the old one in a single day. Clients move across in groups, for example by programme or by region. Architects often call a group like this a cohort. Rules N05 and N14 are written per group, because for each group exactly one system must be in charge, and the group must be able to move back.
Used in:
[aria-label] N05: Only one system can change a record at a time
N05 ·
[aria-label] N14: Every move can be undone, and what is lost is written down
N14 In requirements: NFR-P-005 · NFR-A-008 · INT-023
Hash, digest, hash chain
A digest is a short fingerprint of data that changes if the data changes; a hash chain links records by fingerprint so any tampering shows.
In requirements: FR-008 · NFR-SEC-009 · NFR-C-002
Headroom factor
Extra capacity planned above the measured peak.
In requirements: NFR-P-003 · NFR-S-001
Human decision-maker
A named person with authority who decides, as opposed to the system computing a result. Some decisions must have one by law or policy.
In requirements: BR-005 · FR-003
Idempotent
Safe to repeat: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Payment submission must be idempotent.
In requirements: NFR-A-003 · NFR-I-004
Identity assurance level
How confident the system can be that a person is who they say they are. Level 3 means identity was verified in person or equivalent.
In requirements: FR-027 · FR-088 · NFR-SEC-001 · INT-005
Information Management Act, ARCS and ORCS
The law and the approved schedules (administrative and operational records classification systems) that say how long government records are kept and how they are destroyed.
In requirements: BR-007 · NFR-C-003 · DR-004
Interface
The agreed way one system asks another for information or asks it to do something.
An interface is like a published contract. It says what you can ask for, in what form, and what you get back. Other systems are built to rely on it, so it has to stay stable for a long time.
N10 asks that interfaces use the ministry’s own words, so that the product behind one can be swapped out without anyone who uses it noticing.
Used in:
[aria-label] N10: The interface outlasts the system behind it
N10 ·
[aria-label] N16: Each service has recovery targets, proven in practice runs
N16 In requirements: FR-086 · NFR-P-001 · NFR-A-001 · NFR-M-001 · NFR-I-002 · INT-020
Invalidation, rescission
Invalidation cancels a decision without replacing it, as when the tribunal rescinds one. A new decision then follows separately.
In requirements: FR-059 · DR-002
Issuance run
A scheduled batch of payments with a cutoff, an approval and control totals.
In requirements: BR-004 · FR-009 · NFR-P-002
Issuance Service (payment chokepoint)
The single service every payment must pass through. No other part of the system can send money.
In requirements: FR-042 · FR-060 · FR-097 · NFR-M-006 · INT-001
Judicial review
A court's review of a tribunal decision, the last step after an appeal.
Keeping personal details separately
Storing the details that identify a person in one place, and only a reference to them everywhere else.
Instead of writing a person’s name and details into every record, the history holds a reference number. The details live in one separate store. Deleting them there makes every record that points to them anonymous. Architects call this indirection. It is one of three methods in N12.
Used in:
[aria-label] N12: How records are destroyed is decided before anything is stored
N12 In requirements: NFR-S-002 · DR-004
Lakehouse, analytics platform
One governed store for analysis and reporting, so consumers query data without making new copies.
In requirements: FR-096
Legal time limit
A deadline set in law or policy, such as the time the ministry has to decide.
Many steps in the ministry’s work have a deadline. A client has 20 business days to ask for a reconsideration. The ministry then has 10 business days to decide, or 20 with an approved extension. Some limits count business days and some count calendar days.
Missing some limits changes what the client is owed. That makes them part of the entitlement, not just a service standard, which is why N19 asks the system to track them.
Used in:
[aria-label] N19: The system tracks legal time limits
N19 In requirements: FR-061 · INT-011
Limit on use
A rule that the ministry may hold a piece of information but not use it for a particular purpose.
Holding information lawfully is not the same as being allowed to use it for anything. Policy sometimes bars a use: a detail that must not count in a calculation, content that must not be shared with a certain party, a subject that must not be raised. N21 asks that the limit stays attached to the information, so it goes with every copy and the system can enforce it.
Used in:
[aria-label] N21: Limits on how information may be used travel with it
N21
Migration event
A recorded event saying a record was imported from the old system, rather than inventing events that never happened.
Modern Treaty land
Land held by a First Nation under a modern treaty, where the Nation may run its own assistance program.
In requirements: FR-021 · INT-012
Module (M0–M9)
A stage of delivery in the architecture. Each module is meant to be in use before the next is funded; M0 builds foundations and replaces nothing.
In requirements: BR-004 · BR-014 · NFR-A-005 · INT-013
MoSCoW priority
MUST_HAVE, SHOULD_HAVE, COULD_HAVE and WONT_HAVE: how essential a requirement is.
Moving back (rollback)
Returning a group of clients from the new system to the old one if something goes wrong.
Any large change needs a way back. N14 asks that moving a group back needs no special data project, and that an approved statement lists what information would not survive the trip. The old system cannot hold some of what the new one records, so something is always lost. The question is whether everyone knows what.
Used in:
[aria-label] N14: Every move can be undone, and what is lost is written down
N14 In requirements: FR-047 · NFR-A-006 · NFR-M-006 · DR-015
Non-Crown participant
A party that is not the provincial government, such as an Indigenous governing body acting under its own jurisdiction. Its legal authority is described in its own terms, not as a provincial law section.
In requirements: FR-085 · INT-012
Obligation (OB-)
Something the policy manual requires the ministry to do or not do. The 270 obligations are numbered OB-xx-nn and each is traced to a requirement.
In requirements: BR-013
OCAP
First Nations principles of ownership, control, access and possession of their own data.
OIDC, token exchange
OpenID Connect is the standard sign-in protocol. Token exchange (RFC 8693) passes a user's authority to another organisation; rich authorization requests (RFC 9396) carry the legal basis with it.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-001 · INT-005
Overpayment, administrative error
An overpayment is money paid that was not owed. When the ministry caused it (administrative error), different recovery rules apply.
In requirements: FR-051 · DR-013
p95, p99
The response time that 95% or 99% of requests are faster than.
In requirements: NFR-P-001 · NFR-M-002
Pacific Blue Cross, CLBC, BCANDS
Outside bodies that make some decisions for the ministry: Pacific Blue Cross (dental, optical and hearing supplements), Community Living BC (travel supplement) and the BC Aboriginal Network on Disability Society (on-reserve disability designations).
In requirements: FR-036 · FR-058 · INT-009
Parameter
A rule the design must follow, written so a reviewer can check whether it does.
Each parameter comes with a question you can ask of the running system. If the answer is wrong, the design has broken the rule. There are twenty-one. Each has a code from N01 to N21, which matches the full statement in the architecture documents.
See it at work: Parameters Used in:
[aria-label] N18: Every rule comes with a way to catch it being broken
N18
Part of the system (domain)
One area of the ministry’s work, with its own data and its own rules, such as Payments or Intake.
The new system is built as separate parts, each responsible for one area of the work. Architects call these domains. Each part owns its own data. Parts talk to each other only by sending facts and decisions, never by reaching into each other’s databases.

N21 In requirements: NFR-SEC-008
Partition, partition predicate
Splitting a large table into parts (for example by date) so a query reads only the part it needs.
In requirements: NFR-P-006
Payment instruction
The record of one payment to be made, linked to the decision it pays. It is never edited, only cancelled and replaced.
In requirements: BR-013 · FR-033 · FR-042 · NFR-A-002 · INT-017
PCI-DSS
The card industry's security standard. Keeping card data out of ministry systems keeps them outside its scope.
In requirements: FR-097 · INT-025
PCMS
The Provincial Contract Management System (on Salesforce), which manages service-provider contracts. It is a recent system, likely kept.
In requirements: INT-020
Permanent history (append-only store)
A store where new records are only ever added to the end, and nothing is overwritten.
Instead of changing a record in place, the system adds a new entry saying what changed. That keeps a full history, which is what lets a decision be replayed. But it clashes with the legal duty to destroy some records, and N12 exists to settle that clash before the first record is stored.
Used in:
[aria-label] N12: How records are destroyed is decided before anything is stored
N12
Policy-as-code
Access rules written as versioned, testable code instead of settings changed by hand.
Practice run (recovery exercise)
Deliberately taking a service down to prove it can be brought back within its targets.
A recovery plan that has never been tried is a guess. In a practice run the team simulates a failure, restores the service, and measures how long it took and how much data was lost. N16 counts a recovery target as real only once a practice run has met it.
Used in:
[aria-label] N16: Each service has recovery targets, proven in practice runs
N16
Pre-decision communication
A message giving reasons and a response deadline, stating that no decision has been made yet.
In requirements: FR-006
Prescribed class
A group of people the regulations treat as meeting disability designation without the usual application, often because another body has already assessed them.
In requirements: FR-030
Program policy authority
The ministry role responsible for a program's policy. It approves how rule outputs are classified and accepts what a rollback would lose.
In requirements: BR-014 · FR-003
Protected A, B, C
Canadian government security classifications for sensitive information, with C the most sensitive. Protected C may only be stored on-premise.
In requirements: NFR-P-006 · NFR-C-001 · INT-001 · DR-003
Pure evaluation
A calculation that uses only the inputs it is given, with no clock, database or network calls, so it gives the same answer every time.
In requirements: FR-090
PWD and PPMB
Persons with Disabilities designation and Persons with Persistent Multiple Barriers designation. Each gives access to higher rates or different rules.
RDSP, structured settlement
A Registered Disability Savings Plan; a structured settlement pays compensation in instalments. Both have special treatment in asset rules.
In requirements: FR-017
Reconsideration
A client’s first step to challenge a decision: asking the ministry to look at it again.
A reconsideration is done inside the ministry, by staff who had no part in the original decision. A client usually has 20 business days to ask for one. Some decisions cannot be reconsidered, and N20 asks the system to record which.
Used in:
[aria-label] N17: Different people decide, review and pay
N17 ·
[aria-label] N20: Each benefit records whether and how a decision can be challenged
N20
Reconsideration and Administrative Fairness Unit
The independent ministry unit that makes reconsideration decisions and decides whether reconsideration is available.
In requirements: BR-002 · BR-003 · FR-056 · INT-011
Recovery targets
How quickly a service must be back after a failure, and how much recent data it may lose.
There are two. The recovery time is how long the service may be down before it must be working again. The recovery point is how much recent work may be lost: a recovery point of one hour means at most the last hour of changes. Technical teams call these the RTO and the RPO.
For payments the architecture sets the recovery point at zero: no payment data may be lost at all.
Used in:
[aria-label] N16: Each service has recovery targets, proven in practice runs
N16 In requirements: NFR-A-002
Regression corpus
A set of test cases with known answers that every rules change must still pass.
In requirements: FR-008 · FR-090
Release train
A fixed schedule of software releases that changes must wait for.
In requirements: NFR-A-002
Repayable issuance
Money paid now against a signed promise to repay, which becomes a debt only if a later decision goes against the client.
In requirements: FR-041
Replay
Running a past decision again, from its stored inputs, to show exactly how it was reached.
If a client appeals a decision made years ago, the ministry has to show what it decided and why. Replay means feeding the same rules and the same facts back through the same calculation, and getting exactly the same answer.
That only works if the calculation used nothing but its inputs (N07), and if every input was saved (N08).
See it at work: Determinations Used in:
[aria-label] N07: The calculation uses only what it is given
N07 ·
[aria-label] N08: The decision record is complete on its own
N08 ·
[aria-label] N09: A decision records the moment its facts were read
N09 ·
[aria-label] N11: Buy common tools, and have someone else check any choice to build
N11 ·
[aria-label] N12: How records are destroyed is decided before anything is stored
N12 In requirements: BR-002 · BR-007 · FR-008 · FR-011 · FR-058 · FR-065 · FR-091 · NFR-P-003and 5 more
Replay horizon
How long past decisions can be re-run, and what serves as the record after that.
In requirements: DR-008
Retention schedule
The official list of how long each kind of government record must be kept.
Government records are kept for set periods and then destroyed or archived. A schedule might say case files are kept for a set number of years after the case closes. Deleting a whole kind of record when its time comes is the simplest of the three methods in N12.
Used in:
[aria-label] N12: How records are destroyed is decided before anything is stored
N12
Rules engine
The software that applies the entitlement rules to a client’s facts to reach a decision.
The rules for each benefit are written down in a form a computer can follow. The rules engine takes those rules and a client’s facts, and works out the result. Each version of the rules, and each version of the engine, is kept, so an old decision can be replayed exactly as it was made.
N07 asks that the engine is sealed off: it may use only what it is handed, never the clock, a database or another service.
Used in:
[aria-label] N07: The calculation uses only what it is given
N07 ·
[aria-label] N08: The decision record is complete on its own
N08 In requirements: FR-001 · FR-061 · FR-090 · FR-095
Rules register
The list of every policy rule with its source page, effective dates and status, held apart from the requirements so that dollar amounts and day counts live in one place.
In requirements: BR-014 · FR-010 · FR-016 · FR-037 · FR-048
SBOM, penetration test
A software bill of materials lists every component in a system; a penetration test is an authorised attack to find weaknesses.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-007 · NFR-C-006
Secure Data Exchange
The Province's gateway for sharing personal information between ministries. All cross-ministry traffic goes through it.
In requirements: INT-013
Separation of duties
Making sure no one person controls every step, so each step checks the one before.
Policy sets three separations. The person who reviews a decision cannot be the one who made it. The person who speaks for the ministry at an appeal cannot be either of them. And working out a payment, approving it and releasing it are done by different people. N17 asks the system to enforce these, rather than leaving it to rosters.
Used in:
[aria-label] N17: Different people decide, review and pay
N17 In requirements: BR-004 · FR-047
Set-off
Recovering a debt by deducting it from another amount the ministry owes the same person.
In requirements: FR-048 · FR-052 · FR-060 · INT-007
Severing
Removing protected details from a record before it is released.
A record given to a client can contain information they are not entitled to see, such as details about another person. FOIPPA says which details must be removed first. Doing this by hand on a large record is slow and easy to get wrong. N08 asks that the decision record can be severed on demand.
Used in:
[aria-label] N08: The decision record is complete on its own
N08
Shadow comparison
Running the new system's calculation on the same inputs as the old one and classifying every difference before switching over.
In requirements: BR-001 · INT-023 · DR-003 · DR-014
Shadow root, shadow DOM
A browser feature that hides a component's inner structure. It can break links assistive technology relies on.
In requirements: NFR-U-004
Shred-survivor set
The fixed list of facts that stay readable after a person's records are destroyed, such as payment totals and disclosure records.
In requirements: FR-008 · FR-077 · NFR-C-003 · DR-004
SLO, SLA, error budget
A service level objective or agreement is a stated performance target; the error budget is how much failure the target allows.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-004 · NFR-M-001
SOP (standard operating procedure)
A ministry procedure telling staff how to do a task. SOPs are evidence of current practice, not the authority for a requirement.
Source (provenance)
Where a fact came from: who said it, and which record it was taken from.
Architects call this provenance. It is what lets you judge how far to trust a fact, and what lets a correction find every copy that needs fixing. Once a fact is passed on without it, it cannot be added back later.
Used in:
[aria-label] N02: Parts of the system share facts and decisions, not raw data
N02 ·
[aria-label] N06: Every copy can be traced, and every correction reaches it
N06 In requirements: DR-010
Source hierarchy (Tier 1, 2, 3)
The ranking of sources used to decide what the system must do: Tier 1 is legislation, Tier 2 is the policy manual, Tier 3 is practice (procedures, job aids, spreadsheets). A higher tier wins any conflict.
Statutory administrative decision
A decision made under a law about a person's rights or benefits. It carries a duty to give reasons and a right to challenge.
Statutory basis
The section of a law or regulation that grants an entitlement.
In requirements: BR-003 · FR-092 · FR-099
Statutory decision-maker
The person the law gives authority to make a program's decisions. Only they can approve a class of decisions to be issued without human review.
In requirements: FR-093
Store
A place where data is kept, such as a database.
The new system has many stores. Some are built to answer questions quickly and are refreshed from the main history a moment after it changes. That short delay is normal, but it means a store can be briefly behind. N09 is about what a decision must do about that.
Used in:
[aria-label] N09: A decision records the moment its facts were read
N09
Subsidiary ledger
The ministry's own record of what it owes, pays and recovers, reconciled to the corporate financial system.
In requirements: FR-045 · FR-053 · NFR-U-002
Synchronous, asynchronous
Synchronous means the user waits for the answer; asynchronous means the work is queued and the answer comes later.
In requirements: NFR-A-003
System of record
The one system in charge of a record, whose version counts when there is a disagreement.
While the old and new systems run side by side, the same record may exist in both. N05 says only one of them may change it at a time, for each group of clients. The other system can read it, but cannot write to it.
Used in:
[aria-label] N05: Only one system can change a record at a time
N05 In requirements: FR-047 · NFR-SEC-003
Target architecture
The architecture document (version 2) describing the system that replaces ICM and MIS.
In requirements: FR-099
Telemetry, observability, OpenTelemetry
Data a system emits about its own behaviour (logs, metrics, traces) so problems can be found; OpenTelemetry is the open standard for it.
In requirements: NFR-P-001 · NFR-C-004 · NFR-M-001
TEMPORALLY_UNVERIFIED
A mark on a decision re-run from migrated facts whose recording dates are unknown. It can show an amount but not what the ministry knew at the time.
In requirements: DR-013
The old system (ICM and MIS)
The two systems that do the ministry’s case work today, and that the new system will replace.
ICM, short for Integrated Case Management, is a customer relationship management product adapted for government. MIS is a mainframe built in 1982. The two run side by side and share the core programs between them, so the site calls them together “the old system”.
For years the old and new systems will run side by side while groups of clients move across. The Current State page explains how the work is done today.

N14 In requirements: BR-001 · BR-011 · FR-095 · FR-098 · NFR-P-001 · NFR-S-001 · INT-013 · INT-023
Threat model, runbook
A threat model lists how a part of the system could be attacked; a runbook is a written step-by-step procedure for operations staff.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-008 · NFR-C-006 · NFR-M-006
Three dates (tri-temporal)
Each fact records when it was true, when this system learned it, and, for migrated facts, when the old system recorded it.
Three-way reconciliation
Daily checking that the ministry's ledger, the bank's settlement files and the corporate financial system agree.
In requirements: NFR-P-002
Tier-1 component
A service whose failure stops payments or decisions, covered by 24-hour on-call.
In requirements: BR-013 · NFR-A-002 · NFR-M-006
TLS, mutual TLS, SFTP
Encryption for data in transit. Mutual TLS has both sides prove who they are; SFTP is secure file transfer.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-005 · INT-001
Tombstone
A marker left in place of destroyed data, so replay knows something was there and was lawfully destroyed.
In requirements: NFR-C-003 · DR-004
Transaction time
When the system learned a fact.
This is the date the fact was recorded, which is often later than when it became true. Together with valid time, it lets the ministry answer two separate questions a tribunal will ask: what was true, and what did the ministry know at the time?
See it at work: Evidence Used in:
[aria-label] N01: Every fact is dated and has a source
N01
Transition
The years when the old and new systems run side by side while clients move across.
Replacing a system this size is done in stages. During the transition, some clients are in the new system and some are still in the old one. Most of the risk in a replacement sits here, and several parameters are written for it.
Used in:
[aria-label] N05: Only one system can change a record at a time
N05
Translation layer
Temporary software that lets the new interfaces talk to the old system.
The new interfaces use the ministry’s words. The old system uses its own. The translation layer sits between them and converts one into the other. Architects call it an anti-corruption layer, because it stops the old system’s way of doing things leaking into the new design.
It is meant to be thrown away once the old system is gone. N10 asks that nobody mistakes it for something permanent.
See it at work: Choices Used in:
[aria-label] N10: The interface outlasts the system behind it
N10 ·
[aria-label] N16: Each service has recovery targets, proven in practice runs
N16 In requirements: NFR-P-001 · NFR-A-008 · NFR-I-001 · INT-023
Tribunal
An independent body that hears appeals against ministry decisions.
For most income and disability assistance decisions, this is the Employment and Assistance Appeal Tribunal. Some entitlements go to a different body, which is why N20 records the body for each one.
A tribunal will ask how a decision was reached and what the ministry knew at the time. Several parameters exist so the ministry can answer from the record rather than from memory.
Used in:
[aria-label] N07: The calculation uses only what it is given
N07 ·
[aria-label] N20: Each benefit records whether and how a decision can be challenged
N20 In requirements: INT-011
True-up
Working out, once the real decision is made, the difference between what an emergency payment paid and what was owed.
Valid time
The period during which a fact was true in the world.
A client’s income of $1,100 might be true from March to June. That period is its valid time. It is separate from when the ministry found out, which is transaction time. Keeping both lets the ministry recalculate the past correctly when it learns something late.
See it at work: Evidence Used in:
[aria-label] N01: Every fact is dated and has a source
N01 In requirements: DR-001 · DR-010
Variant
A version of an entitlement with its own conditions, such as a supplement for one group of clients.
Some entitlements come in several forms. A variant can differ from its parent in who hears an appeal, or even in whether it can be reconsidered at all. N20 records these details for each variant, and never copies them from the parent.
Used in:
[aria-label] N20: Each benefit records whether and how a decision can be challenged
N20 In requirements: BR-003 · FR-033 · FR-092
Watermark
A marker recording exactly how far through the system’s history a decision read.
The system’s history is a numbered list of events. The watermark is the number of the last event a decision saw. Writing it into the decision record shows exactly which version of the facts the decision was based on. Setting a limit on how far behind a store may be stops a decision being made from an out-of-date view.
Used in:
[aria-label] N09: A decision records the moment its facts were read
N09 In requirements: FR-001 · FR-058 · NFR-P-004
Work item
A task assigned to a person or team, with a due date, priority and history.
In requirements: FR-009 · FR-014 · FR-028 · FR-038 · FR-044 · FR-059 · FR-067 · FR-071and 6 more
Write-back
Copying changes from the new system back into the old one so its reports and interfaces keep working during the move.
In requirements: NFR-SEC-011 · NFR-M-003 · INT-023 · DR-014

Glossary
A PWD* designation granted in July.
It takes effect from March.
Four months of payments were right when the ministry made them. They are now an underpayment: four months a client went without money they turn out to have been owed. The current system keeps only today's answer. It rewrites history instead of recording it. What did we know, when did we know it, and how do we prove it? This design keeps all three.

The month being asked about
